assessment.nobel_worthiness: A consequential account of how technology, trade exposure and task change reshape labour demand and inequality, with wide influence on empirical labour economics and policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson form a coherent core for the trade-shock and task-based empirical contribution.
assessment.maturity: The evidence base and its conceptual influence have accumulated over a substantial period.
uncertainties: The discovery combines several mechanisms, making a single prize formulation potentially broad.
Credit boundaries relative to wider research on technological change and trade remain contestable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale measurement of intergenerational mobility has changed both the empirical agenda and understanding of place, inequality and opportunity.
assessment.attribution: Chetty, Hendren and Friedman are a defensible core for the administrative-data mobility program.
assessment.maturity: The research program has generated a sustained body of results and extensive follow-on work.
uncertainties: The work is comparatively recent for a prize.
The appropriate attribution among the broader collaborating research network is difficult.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Audit and correspondence designs made discrimination measurable in real labour-market settings and supplied unusually direct evidence on a major economic and social question.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan are central to the influential modern experimental demonstration; the listed field has broader antecedents.
assessment.maturity: The approach has been replicated, adapted and used across markets over many years.
uncertainties: Audit studies identify particular margins of discrimination and need careful interpretation beyond the experimental setting.
Attribution between seminal individual studies and the wider audit-study tradition is not straightforward.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The modern analysis of monopsony gave labour-market institutions and employer wage-setting power a more persuasive theoretical and empirical framework.
assessment.attribution: Manning is an especially clear intellectual focal point for the modern monopsony contribution.
assessment.maturity: The framework is well established and has become central to empirical and policy analysis of labour markets.
uncertainties: The listed discovery spans theory and a rapidly expanding empirical literature with diffuse credit.
Empirical magnitudes and mechanisms vary considerably across labour markets.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Research on early-life conditions and skill formation has demonstrated the long economic reach of health and developmental environments, with major implications for policy evaluation.
assessment.attribution: Currie, Almond and Cunha represent complementary empirical and dynamic-framework contributions to the stated discovery.
assessment.maturity: The central findings have been developed across multiple cohorts, settings and methods.
uncertainties: The candidate combines related but distinct contributions rather than one sharply delimited discovery.
Causal interpretation can depend on setting-specific identification assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification fundamentally clarified what data can and cannot establish under credible weak assumptions, improving the discipline's treatment of uncertainty.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the unmistakable central figure in the foundational contribution; the listed co-contributors extend the program.
assessment.maturity: The framework is longstanding, technically mature and influential across applied econometrics.
uncertainties: Its practical policy impact is less easily summarized than that of some empirical discoveries.
A prize formulation would need to distinguish foundational partial identification from later methodological extensions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural modelling of labour supply and household behaviour has provided a durable way to evaluate taxation and welfare reforms when behavioural responses matter.
assessment.attribution: Blundell, Meghir and MaCurdy are appropriate leading contributors to the specified structural labour-supply tradition.
assessment.maturity: The methods have had long-standing influence in public and labour economics.
uncertainties: Structural conclusions can be sensitive to modelling restrictions and data environments.
The contribution overlaps with a broad literature on dynamic discrete choice and household behaviour.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic-panel GMM made credible analysis of persistent outcomes with individual heterogeneity feasible in a vast range of economic applications.
assessment.attribution: Arellano and Bond provide the clearest core attribution for the named estimator and its canonical application.
assessment.maturity: The contribution is highly mature, broadly taught and extensively used.
uncertainties: The prize case rests on an econometric tool whose applied use can be unreliable under weak instruments or specification choices.
Later methodological developments complicate a narrow attribution.
